interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on formula cards whose letters wear their units or example values, each formula's steps drawn as a flow diagram from the letter you want and undone right to left, and a check that puts numbers which fit the old formula into the new one, some screens showing an idea and the rest asking you to try it.
interactive.ignores: The amounts (12 V, 3 A and 4 Ω; 16 V, 2 A and 8 Ω; 2300 W, 230 V and 10 A; and the numbers in v = u + at and y = 3x + 5) are example values, chosen so the checks come out whole or simple. The letters in v = u + at are worked as letters only, without units. Undoing in another order can also work when every term is treated; the lesson walks back from the last step. Squares and square roots are the next lesson, and expanding brackets waits for a later course.

numbers.label: V = IR drawn from I is one step, × R, undone by ÷ R to give I = V ÷ R, in step 1
V = IR drawn from R is one step, × I, undone by ÷ I to give R = V ÷ I, not − I or × I, in step 2
12 V, 3 A and 4 Ω fit V = IR, since 3 × 4 = 12; I = V ÷ R gives 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and R = V ÷ I gives 12 ÷ 3 = 4, in step 3
I = V ÷ R with 16 V, 2 A and 8 Ω: V = I × R gives 2 × 8 = 16, not 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25 or 2 + 8 = 10, in step 4

y = 3x + 5 becomes x = (y − 5) ÷ 3, and y = 26 gives (26 − 5) ÷ 3 = 7, in step 7

explain.text:
A formula is an equation with letters for its amounts, so you change its subject, the letter on its own, the same way you solve an equation. Draw the steps done to the letter you want, then undo them on both sides in reverse, each with its opposite. In V = IR, V is I times R, so dividing both sides by R gives I = V ÷ R, and dividing both sides by I gives R = V ÷ I. Ohm's law, V = IR, and power, P = VI, are the two equations the other power formulas are built from,[^1] and P = VI turns round the same way into I = P ÷ V. A formula with a sum and a product can take two steps. In v = u + at, the steps done to t are × a and then + u, so undo the + u first and the × a second, giving t = (v − u) ÷ a. The brackets make the whole of v − u be divided. Without them, t = v − u ÷ a divides only the u, and with v = 18, u = 6 and a = 3 it gives 16 where t is 4.

To check a new formula, put in numbers that fit the old one. 12 V, 3 A and 4 Ω fit V = IR, and I = V ÷ R gives 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so both sides match. The units agree too, since volts ÷ ohms gives amps. The shortcut "change side, change sign" works perfectly for a great number of equations.[^2] It gives the right answer when the step that crosses over is a + or a −, so v = u + at becomes u = v − at. With a × it fails. It turns V = IR into I = V − R, and 12 − 4 = 8, not 3, while volts take away ohms makes no sense. Bitesize's National 5 notes give the general rule as change side, change operation,[^3] so a × crossing over becomes ÷, the same as undoing it on both sides. Undoing a divide by dividing again fails as well. One recorded slip reaches x ÷ 4 = 160 correctly and then writes x = 160 ÷ 4,[^4] and from I = V ÷ R with 2 A and 8 Ω, V = I ÷ R gives 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25 where V is 16 V.

**Change a formula's subject by undoing the steps done to that letter, last step first, on both sides, so V = IR gives I = V ÷ R and v = u + at gives t = (v − u) ÷ a. Change side, change sign works only for + and −. Check a new formula with numbers that fit the old one.**

practice.text:
**Rule of thumb:** Draw the steps done to the letter you want. Undo them from the last back to the first, on both sides, each with its opposite, then check with numbers that fit the old formula.

**Worked example:** Make I the subject of P = VI. I is multiplied by V, so divide both sides by V, giving I = P ÷ V. As a check, 2300 W at 230 V gives 2300 ÷ 230 = 10 A, and 230 × 10 = 2300.

**Common mistakes**
- Change side, change sign on a ×. The shortcut works for a great number of equations,[^2] but it turns P = VI into I = P − V, and 2300 − 230 = 2070, not 10. Change the operation instead, so × becomes ÷.[^3]
- Undoing a divide by dividing again. One recorded slip reaches x ÷ 4 = 160 and then writes x = 160 ÷ 4.[^4] From I = V ÷ R, multiply both sides by R to get V = I × R, not V = I ÷ R.

interactive.html:
A formula's steps on a flow diagram, undone backwards to change its subject, then checked with numbers.

Undo the steps done to the letter you want, last first, then check with numbers. The amounts are example values.
interactive.title: Rearranging formulas
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a formula's steps drawn as a flow diagram from the letter you want and undone right to left, last step first, each box lighting as its opposite undoes it, when you make a different letter the subject of V = IR, P = VI or v = u + at, with numbers that fit the old formula put into the new one as a check, so that change side, change sign on a × fails its check in red.

checks.label: Every new formula undoes its old one and gives back the letter's example value: I = V ÷ R, R = V ÷ I, V = I × R, I = P ÷ V, x = (y − 5) ÷ 3, t = (v − u) ÷ a, u = v − at, a = (v − u) ÷ t, V = P ÷ I; every card's values fit it, 12 = 3 × 4, 16 = 2 × 8, 2300 = 230 × 10, 26 = 3 × 7 + 5, 18 = 6 + 3 × 4; and v = 20, u = 8, a = 4 give t = 3, with 8 + 4 × 3 = 20

They all are combinations of just two equations, Ohm's law and power: V = IR put into P = VI gives P = I²R for the amounts on every electrical card, with R = V ÷ I where a card has no R (23 Ω for 2300 W at 230 V)

The change side, change sign method works absolutely perfectly for a great number of equations: wherever the step that crosses over is a + or a −, it gives the same new formula as undoing on both sides

To change the subject of a formula the terms are rearranged following the general rule, change side, change operation: each step crossing over as its opposite operation, last step first, gives every new formula on these screens, and every check matches
Reach the equation x / 4 = 160 correctly, then x = 160/4: dividing where it should multiply gives 40, and 40 / 4 is 10, not 160; multiplying gives 640, and 640 / 4 = 160

Each puzzle accepts only its own answer, and every wrong answer offered is the one a named slip gives, its check failing: change side, change sign used on a × or a ÷; a step done again instead of undone; a divide the wrong way round; only part of a side divided; or the × undone before the +

Every picture, finished, draws the steps in order from the letter wanted, each undo box under the step it undoes with the opposite steps lit, then the new formula and its check; the change side screen fails its check and units in the warning colour; and a wrong answer's formula and check fail in the warning colour, clear of the check's name
Before an answer, nothing in a puzzle's picture shows the answer: no undo box lit, no new formula, no value for the letter

Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion within 2.5 s and a slip within 1 s; parts start at least 0.45 s apart

applied.problem: "A formula with a sum in it takes two steps" is too general: u = v − at from the same formula takes one step (screen 9). Also the slip 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25 uses 2 and 8 without saying they are 2 A and 8 Ω, so read alone on review the numbers come from nowhere.
Not every card's letters wear units: the v = u + at and y = 3x + 5 cards carry example values only (ignores says so), and the electrical cards after the first screens show values with units.

notes.problem: Every number is kind "constant", but 12 V, 3 A, 4 Ω, 16 V, 2 A, 8 Ω, 2300 W, 230 V, 10 A and the v = u + at and y = 3x + 5 values are example values chosen for whole checks (ignores says so), so their kind should be "assumed"; frozen, so recorded here.
